fields.description: Five questions covering the same topics on every attempt. Pass with at least three correct.

fields.title: A Place Is Not a Participant List
fields.content:
A historical place name helps locate an action, but it does not identify every person who took part. A town could include leaders, participants, residents affected by events and people whose actions are not recorded. These groups can overlap. Being present in a place is not the same as joining a movement.

Use a modern evidence desk with three fictional cards: a place label, a named action and an account of an affected household. The place label tells you where to investigate. The named action helps identify participation. The household account would help examine an experience. These are teaching categories, not authentic registers for the cases in this mission. To describe a community fairly, say which people and actions your source actually records. Do not decide a persons role or motive from a modern regional label, religion or ancestry. An unnamed person is not automatically a nonparticipant either.

fields.title: One Island, Different Movements
fields.content:
CulturEd places Tamblots uprising in Bohol in 1621. It also describes the movement associated with Dagohoy in Bohol from 1744 to 1829. One place can therefore contain different movements at different times. Put separate case cards on your timeline rather than merging every Bohol action into one continuous event.

The earlier case is connected in its account with religious practice; the later account describes a burial dispute and local organization. These short summaries do not supply every participants beliefs. Similar themes do not prove that the same people joined both movements or that they followed one unchanged plan. The beginnings are more than a century apart. Ask the same questions of each case: when, where, who is recorded and what action or concern is described? Respect peoples beliefs while investigating particular actions. This activity asks for evidence comparison, not religious practice or a judgement about which belief is better.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then return to the evidence before practice.

fields.title: Read a Claim About Wider Reach
fields.content:
The NHCP marker for Agustin Sumuroy connects the Palapag uprising of 1 June 1649 with forced labor and abuses. It also describes spread beyond the starting place, naming areas in the Visayas, Mindanao and Luzon. This lets us investigate a movement with a wider reported reach rather than treating every case as limited to one town.

Keep the wording of the source in view. Reported spread is not a census of every participant or proof that all communities acted together in the same way. A marker written later summarizes a history; it does not supply every local meeting or account of coordination. To investigate a named area more closely, seek records about the actions and people there. Our teaching card lists broad island groups rather than pretending to reconstruct exact routes of travel or command. A line between places on a diagram would not by itself prove who carried a message or how every action was organized.

fields.title: A Named Contribution in Ilocos
fields.content:
The NHCP registry records that Gabriela Silang continued the Ilocos uprising after Diego Silang. This identifies a contribution in a particular regional setting. It helps a comparison include leadership changes instead of treating a region as one person or an unchanged group. A regional account can contain different people and stages.

Use the contribution as evidence of the named action. Do not turn it into a complete register of Ilocos residents or assume that everyone supported the same aims. A leader and a whole community are not interchangeable. The later marker also cannot tell us every unnamed persons role. When comparing this case with Bohol or Palapag, identify what each source actually supplies: a leadership continuation, a movement period or a statement of spread. These are different clues. Additional records would be needed to describe every contributor or establish coordination between separate cases. Regional variety belongs in the explanation rather than being erased.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then return to the evidence before practice.

fields.title: Build a Community Evidence Portfolio
fields.content:
Build a portfolio with columns for case, place, period, recorded action and limits. Place Tamblot and the Dagohoy movement on separate Bohol rows. Add the reported spread from the Sumuroy marker and the named leadership continuation in Ilocos. These entries let you recognize different regional experiences without pretending that the sources provide the same detail for each.

A useful portfolio can reveal questions, not only answers. Which account names participants? Which describes a wider reach? Which leaves local coordination unclear? A common concern is worth comparing, but it does not automatically establish one national organization. Do not rank regions by bravery, participation totals you do not have or battles won. Missing detail in a short source does not make a community less important. The next mission will examine women and Indigenous peoples more closely. Keep roles connected to evidence rather than assigning them from identity or asking classmates to disclose family background.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then return to the evidence before practice.
